paragraphs.title: The Degradation of What Was Precious and Jerusalem's Famine

easy.explanation: They are described as comparable to fine gold.
easy.q: What are the precious sons of Zion compared to?

answers: No man broke bread for them
They were sent to the fields
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “no man breaketh it unto them.”
easy.q: What happened to the children who asked for bread?

easy.explanation: Those who once ate delicately were desolate in the streets.
easy.q: Where did those who had fed delicately become desolate?

answers: From wealth and honor to hunger and humiliation
From the wilderness to the sea
medium.explanation: The passage moves from gold and fine clothing to hunger, streets, and refuse.
medium.q: What major contrast appears in verses 1–8?

answers: An improvement in the people's condition
A decline in status and condition
A change in the potter's work
medium.explanation: The comparison shows how greatly the precious people had been brought low.
medium.q: What does the comparison between gold and earthen pitchers emphasize?

medium.explanation: The word describes people left in misery and ruin.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “desolate” mean in “They that did feed delicately are desolate”?

answers: From wealth and beauty to hunger and physical decay
challenge.explanation: The passage progresses from gold and beauty to thirst, hunger, and skin cleaving to bones.
challenge.q: How does the description of humiliation develop through verses 1–8?

answers: The severity of hunger and dehydration
challenge.explanation: The image shows the extreme physical effects of famine.
challenge.q: What does the image of the skin cleaving to the bones emphasize?

answers: Even normally nurturing mothers are described as failing to care for their young
The women willingly left the city
challenge.explanation: The comparison presents the breakdown of normal care during the disaster.
challenge.q: Why does the comparison with ostriches strengthen the description of the crisis?

paragraphs.title: The Agony of Famine and the City's Destruction

easy.explanation: The verse says those slain with the sword are better than those slain with hunger.
easy.q: Who are said to be better off?

answers: They sent their children to the nations
They hid their children in the palace
easy.explanation: The KJV says their children became their meat.
easy.q: What did the pitiful women do in the extreme famine?
What did the fire in Zion devour?

answers: Famine victims suffer prolonged and severe agony
medium.explanation: The verse emphasizes the painful wasting caused by hunger.
medium.q: Why are those slain with the sword described as better off than those slain with hunger?

answers: Both describe the depth and extremity of the disaster
The first describes victory and the second celebration
The first concerns rain and the second trade
medium.explanation: Extreme famine and consuming fire together display the city's devastation.
medium.q: How do verses 9–10 connect with verses 11–12?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes people weakened and afflicted by famine.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “stricken through” mean in this passage?

answers: From the suffering of individuals to the destruction of Zion as a whole
From the city’s ruin to its success
From the enemy to a national celebration
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from famine victims to the fire consuming Zion.
challenge.q: What is the main movement from verse 9 to verse 11?

answers: The destruction was beyond what anyone expected
challenge.explanation: Even rulers and inhabitants of the world could not have imagined the enemy entering Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What does “The kings of the earth...would not have believed” emphasize?

answers: Famine destroys the people while fire destroys the city
They represent material and spiritual riches
challenge.explanation: The people suffer physically, while the city's foundations are consumed.
challenge.q: How do famine and fire form one picture of destruction?

paragraphs.title: The Sins of the Leaders and Defilement in the Streets

easy.explanation: The passage names the sins of the prophets and the iniquities of the priests.
easy.q: Whose sins are given as the reason for the destruction?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “They have wandered as blind men in the streets.”
easy.q: How did the people wander in the streets?

easy.explanation: They were told, “Depart ye; it is unclean.”
easy.q: What were the unclean people told?

answers: Shed the blood of the just
medium.explanation: Their sins included shedding the blood of righteous people.
medium.q: What had the prophets and priests done?

answers: Blood shows the destruction, while uncleanness brings rejection and separation
They describe an abundance of food
medium.explanation: Violence has polluted the city, and the polluted people are driven away.
medium.q: How are blood and uncleanness related in the passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes moral and ceremonial defilement caused by bloodshed.
medium.q: What does “polluted themselves with blood” mean?

answers: The prophets and priests bore moral responsibility for the condition
They were the only people living in the city
They ruled only over the fields
challenge.explanation: The passage connects the leaders' sins with the bloodshed and ruin of the city.
challenge.q: Why are the sins of the leaders presented as an explanation for the destruction?

answers: Their position did not protect them from losing honor
They became rulers of the city
challenge.explanation: The anger of the LORD meant that even priests and elders were not favored.
challenge.q: What does the rejection of the priests and elders show about their status?

answers: Confusion, lack of direction, and inability to escape
challenge.explanation: The image portrays people unable to find a safe or clear way through the crisis.
challenge.q: What does the image of blind men emphasize about the city?

paragraphs.title: False Hopes, Siege, and the Captured King

easy.explanation: They watched for a nation that could not save them.
easy.q: From whom did the people hope for help?

answers: They hunted their steps so they could not go in the streets
easy.explanation: The enemies hunted their steps and prevented movement in the streets.
easy.q: What did the enemies do to their movements through the city?

easy.explanation: The anointed of the LORD, described as the breath of their nostrils, was captured.
easy.q: Who was caught in the enemies' pits?

answers: The nation they watched for could not save them
medium.explanation: The verse explicitly says they watched for a nation that could not save them.
medium.q: Why did the people's hope in the nations prove vain?

answers: The people could not escape and were overtaken
medium.explanation: The closed streets and pursuit made escape impossible.
medium.q: What was the result of the enemies hunting their steps?

medium.explanation: The pits represent the enemies' traps or snares.
medium.q: What does “caught in their pits” mean?

answers: While the people wait for help, the enemies close in and prevent escape
Waiting allows the people to win
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from futile expectation to pursuit, capture, and death.
challenge.q: How does the pursuit connect with the people's vain hope?

answers: He was regarded as a source of life and protection
He was unrelated to the people
challenge.explanation: The expression shows how greatly the people depended on the king.
challenge.q: What does the title “the breath of our nostrils” suggest about the king?

answers: The one regarded as the people's protector was himself captured
The person who escaped returned victorious
challenge.explanation: The king under whose shadow they hoped to live was caught in the enemy's trap.
challenge.q: What is ironic about the capture of the king?

paragraphs.title: Mockery of Edom and the End of Zion's Punishment

easy.explanation: The verse addresses the daughter of Edom dwelling in the land of Uz.
easy.q: To whom is the lament addressed in verse 21?

easy.explanation: The cup is said to pass through to Edom.
easy.q: What will also come to Edom?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished.”
easy.q: What is said about the iniquity of the daughter of Zion?

answers: Edom faces judgment, while Zion's punishment is accomplished
Zion is punished while Edom is rewarded
medium.explanation: The passage announces judgment for Edom but an end to Zion's captivity.
medium.q: What contrast appears between Edom and Zion at the end?

answers: Edom will suffer judgment and be exposed
Edom will find refuge from Zion
medium.explanation: The words continue the image of drinking the cup of judgment.
medium.q: What does “thou shalt be drunken, and shalt make thyself naked” mean in context?

answers: He will call the sin to account and judge it
medium.explanation: The phrase means that Edom's sin will be remembered and punished.
medium.q: What does “he will visit thine iniquity” mean?

answers: Edom is told to rejoice, but judgment is immediately announced
The address has nothing to do with judgment
challenge.explanation: The apparent invitation to rejoice contrasts with the coming cup of judgment.
challenge.q: Why is the address to Edom ironic?

answers: The end of the captivity described in the passage
challenge.explanation: The statement promises that Zion will not be carried away again into captivity.
challenge.q: What does “he will no more carry thee away into captivity” express about Zion?

answers: It turns from Zion's suffering to Edom's judgment and Zion's restored hope
It turns from war to ordinary daily life
It turns from wealth to rebuilding the temple
challenge.explanation: The final verses look toward Edom's accountability and the end of Zion's exile.
challenge.q: How does the ending change the focus of the lament?
